topic.title: where they were somebody
topic.claim: You moved your parents to your city to look after them. They lost the only place where they were somebody.
topic.moment: Papa sits on your sofa in a city where no shopkeeper knows his name, waiting for you to come home.

turn.believed: Bringing them to your city is the loving, obvious way to care for them.
turn.actually: You added years of safety and subtracted the whole world where they mattered.

topic.because: Back home papa was the man people greeted, mummy had her lane and her people. In your city they're just your parents, dependent and nameless, waiting on your schedule.
topic.payoff: You gave them a safer life and a smaller one. In your city they're safe. Back home, they were someone.
topic.feeling: the guilt hidden inside a good decision
topic.villain: the arrangement where care and belonging live in two different cities
topic.behaviour: adult kids relocate ageing parents to their own city for convenience and safety
topic.mechanism: the move trades their standing and community for your proximity, so they gain safety and lose the place they mattered
topic.group: adults who moved parents to live near them
topic.send_to: a friend weighing whether to bring their parents to the city
topic.why_now: post-Diwali, when many families make the 'move them here' decision

cover.headline: Moving your parents to your city costs them [their standing]
cover.sub: Closer to you, safer, and known to no one here

paragraphs: You moved your parents into your city to care for them.
They lost the only place they were somebody.
slides.why_swipe: How can a caring decision cost them something?

paragraphs: A hospital ten minutes away, a lift instead of stairs, you in the next room. Everyone agreed over Diwali. Even your parents.
Parents rarely say no to this, because no sounds like refusing your love.
slides.why_swipe: So what did they actually give up?

paragraphs: Back home, in the small town or the old colony, people knew them. A ten-minute walk to the market took an hour of hellos.
A truck can move the almirah. It can't move the people who knew them.
slides.why_swipe: What does their day look like in your city?

paragraphs: Here, the society guard asks them for a flat number whenever they step out for milk. The lift goes up and down all day, full of people who don't say hello.
slides.why_swipe: So who are they to people here?

paragraphs: Here, the neighbours call them "1204 waale uncle-aunty." The move changed who they are to other people, not just where they sit.
slides.why_swipe: So was the move a mistake?

paragraphs: This doesn't make the move wrong. Falls happen.
At 75, in a town with one good doctor, a fall at night means a long drive to the nearest real hospital.
slides.why_swipe: Then who does the move really help?

paragraphs: What you gain is peace of mind. You stop dreading the phone ringing late at night.
And their day now runs on your calendar. Your father rereads the newspaper on the sofa, the TV kept low in your house. Your mother's evening starts when your key turns.
slides.why_swipe: So how are they really doing?

paragraphs: Ask how they're settling in and you'll hear "Hum theek hain, beta." Then they ask what time you'll be home.
You gave them a safer life and a smaller one.

end.save: Read it again before you book the movers for your parents.
end.send: Send to the friend who came back from Diwali saying 'I'm bringing them here this year.'

draft.caption: We brought them closer and somehow made their world smaller, and both of those are true.
draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text post arguing that when adult children move ageing parents to their own city, the parents gain safety but lose the place where they were known. A nearby hospital, a lift and the child in the next room make everyone agree over Diwali, and parents rarely say no because no sounds like refusing their child's love. Back home, a walk to the market took an hour of hellos. In the new city the guard asks for a flat number, the lift is full of strangers, and neighbours call them '1204 waale uncle-aunty'. It admits the move isn't wrong, since a fall at night in a town with one good doctor is a real risk. The child gains peace of mind, while the parents' day runs on the child's calendar: the father rereads the newspaper with the TV kept low, the mother's evening starts when the key turns. It ends: they say 'Hum theek hain, beta', ask what time you'll be home, and you gave them a safer life and a smaller one.
